clue.text: Slides of hunting parties, say

indicators.note: say tells us the word for hunting parties is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: shoots are organised gatherings for shooting game

explanation.surface: Someone notes that groups out hunting slide about, as it were.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks the sound-alike: SHOOTS, outings to shoot game birds, is pronounced just like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Chutes are sloping channels down which people or goods slide, so they are slides.

clue.text: Woman's song about botanist's first plant collections

indicators.note: about means the woman's song goes around the next letter

parts.note: her is the woman's possessive
an aria is an operatic song

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of botanist's is taken

explanation.surface: A woman sings about a botanist's first specimen collection.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbaria are archives of dried pressed plant specimens kept for study.

clue.text: Get a lute repaired for teaching

indicators.note: repaired suggests the letters of get a lute are fixed into a new order

explanation.surface: Have your lute mended so that you can take lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repaired' rearranges GETALUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutelage is instruction or guardianship given by a tutor.

clue.text: Prophecy by Sally about cricket side

indicators.note: about means the sally wraps round the cricket side

parts.note: a sally is a sortie, a sudden military dash out
the leg side is one half of a cricket field

explanation.surface: A forecast made by an outing round the cricket ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The leg side in cricket is the half of the field behind the batsman's legs; a sally is a sudden dash out by troops under siege.
explanation.definitionFit: Sortilege is divination by drawing lots, a form of foretelling.

clue.text: Walks awkwardly to the mess

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles clumsily off to the officers' dining hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mess' suggests an army dining room, but the second sense is a chaotic muddle.
explanation.definitionFit: To shamble is to shuffle along clumsily; a shambles is a scene of total disorder.

clue.text: Substitute tax I go on about, to great acclamation

parts.note: a stand-in is a substitute

indicators.note: about means go on is placed around tax and I

parts.note: VAT is value added tax

explanation.surface: A replacement levy keeps being complained about, to loud applause.
explanation.definitionFit: A standing ovation is an audience rising to its feet in applause, the warmest acclaim.

clue.text: Pacify a woman out of condition

indicators.note: out of here means the woman is outside, enclosing the condition

parts.note: Molly is a woman's name
if introduces a condition

explanation.surface: Calming a woman who is unfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of condition' wants to mean unfit, but 'out of' is the container signal and 'condition' is the conditional word.
explanation.definitionFit: To mollify is to soothe or appease someone's anger.

clue.text: Security nil at first, but the temple may back it

indicators.note: at first places the word for nil in front of the word for security

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring
a lock provides security

explanation.surface: Security is nothing at first, but a church might support it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'temple' is not a church: it is the side of the head, where a lovelock of hair hangs.
explanation.definitionFit: A lovelock is a curl of hair worn hanging at the side of the head, which that spot would carry.

clue.text: Serviceman who painted or conducted, do we hear?

indicators.note: do we hear signals that a name sounding like the soldier's rank is meant

parts.note: John Singer Sargent painted portraits and Sir Malcolm Sargent conducted orchestras

explanation.surface: A question about a soldier who was also an artist or conductor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do we hear' marks the sound-alike: SARGENT, both painter and conductor, sounds like the rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant is a non-commissioned officer in the armed forces.

clue.text: Review backing river standards

parts.note: crit is short for criticism, a review

indicators.note: backing means the river's name is read backwards

parts.note: the Aire is a Yorkshire river

explanation.surface: A critique supports the standards of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns AIRE into ERIA. The Aire is a river in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Criteria are principles or tests used for judging.

clue.text: Bird to cherish in Puerto Rico

indicators.note: in means the word for cherish sits inside the abbreviation

parts.note: to love is to cherish

explanation.surface: A bird beloved in the Caribbean island.
explanation.definitionFit: The plover is a wading shorebird.

clue.text: Judge has trouble with sentence for old lag

parts.note: to ail is to trouble
bird is slang for a prison term, from rhyming bird-lime = time

explanation.surface: A judge struggles to sentence a habitual offender.
explanation.walkthrough: BIRD for a prison sentence is British slang. An old lag is a long-standing convict.
explanation.definitionFit: A jailbird is a habitual prisoner, someone often locked up.

clue.text: Breather that's part of his prey

definitions.text: Breather that's part of his prey

parts.note: a gill is the breathing organ of a fish
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: The breathing organ of a fish forms part of what a hunter's assistant pursues.
explanation.walkthrough: A gillie is a Scottish attendant on a fishing or hunting trip; his prey is the fish, of which the gill is part.
explanation.definitionFit: A gillie attends sportsmen fishing for salmon, whose breathing organ belongs to that catch.

clue.text: Holiday island gives us energy for high jinks

indicators.note: for high jinks suggests the letters of us energy cavort into a new order

explanation.surface: A holiday spot gives us lots of energy for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for high jinks' rearranges USENERGY.
explanation.definitionFit: Guernsey is one of the Channel Islands, a resort off Normandy.

clue.text: Riot ideal material for article

indicators.note: material is read as raw stuff out of which the letters of riot ideal are remade

explanation.surface: An ideal disturbance becomes stuff for a newspaper piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'material' rearranges RIOTIDEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: An editorial is a newspaper's leading opinion piece.

clue.text: Break in, being unafraid of human contact

explanation.surface: Taming an animal so it no longer fears people.
explanation.definitionFit: To tame a horse is to break it in; a tame creature is used to people and not wild.

clue.text: Large number imprisoned in the Moroccan capital?

annotationWithheld.why: Large number imprisoned in the Moroccan capital? (8): scan confirms the text, but no parse found; possibly M (thousand) as the capital of Moroccan, yet 'imprisoned in' is unexplained
annotationWithheld.clue: Large number imprisoned in the Moroccan capital?

clue.text: Feeble sentimentality with scope to grow rapidly

parts.note: mush is soppy sentimentality
room is scope or space

explanation.surface: Soppy feeling given space to expand quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: To mushroom is to expand or spread suddenly, like fungi overnight.

clue.text: Son with small fiddle in satirical sketch

parts.note: a kit is a small violin once used by dancing masters

explanation.surface: A boy plays a little violin in a comic sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: KIT is an old word for a small pocket violin.
explanation.definitionFit: A skit is a short humorous parody or sketch.

clue.text: Voluptuary upset by cutting appeal ceremony

indicators.note: cutting means the overturned by divides the appeal

parts.note: SA is sex appeal

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means the word by is turned over

parts.note: a rite is a ceremony

explanation.surface: A pleasure-seeker is annoyed by an appeal interrupting a ritual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' in a down clue turns the little word over, giving YB, which 'cutting' then lodges in the appeal.
explanation.definitionFit: A sybarite is someone devoted to luxury and sensual pleasure.

clue.text: Angry when equipment is dropped in water?

indicators.note: is dropped in means the equipment goes inside the word for angry

parts.note: irate means angry
a rig is equipment

explanation.surface: Fury when gear is dropped into water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'water' is a verb here, not the stuff the gear falls into.
explanation.definitionFit: To irrigate fields is to supply them with water.

clue.text: Speed to centre of 10, perhaps — a large town

annotationWithheld.why: Speed to centre of 10, perhaps - a large town (8): CITY is clear, but no parse of 'to centre of 10, perhaps' gives VELO from 10-across PLOVER
annotationWithheld.clue: Speed to centre of 10, perhaps — a large town

clue.text: The rascal's evil is to no purpose

indicators.note: is here reads as is in, since evil is in vain, so the bad word sits inside the pointless one

parts.note: in vain means to no purpose
ill means evil

explanation.surface: A scoundrel's wickedness comes to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The everyday phrase for futility, 'in vain', is doing the placing: evil sits within the pointless word.
explanation.definitionFit: A villain is a scoundrel or wrongdoer.

clue.text: "Mongst horrid shapes, and shrieks, and sights" (Milton)

definitions.text: "Mongst horrid shapes, and shrieks, and sights" (Milton)

parts.words: "Mongst horrid shapes, and shrieks, and sights" (Milton)
parts.note: the missing last word of this line from Milton's poem L'Allegro, describing a hellish scene

explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the blank: the line from L'Allegro ends with a word meaning wicked or godless.
explanation.definitionFit: The quoted line ends with a word for sinful or ungodly things.

clue.text: An idealist with no end of vision sounds barmy!

indicators.note: with no means a letter is dropped from the idealist

parts.note: a romantic is an idealist

indicators.note: end of means only the last letter of vision is taken

explanation.surface: A dreamer without sight seems crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' removes N (the end of vision) from A ROMANTIC. 'barmy' means mad, but sounds like balmy, fragrant.
explanation.definitionFit: Balmy air is fragrant, scented like spices, and barmy is said the same in British speech.

clue.text: In Alaska, a woman's hooded jacket

indicators.note: In means the abbreviation for Alaska goes round the woman

parts.note: AK is the postal code for Alaska
Nora is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A woman in Alaska owns a hooded coat.
explanation.definitionFit: An anorak is a waterproof hooded parka, from an Inuit word.

clue.text: One irregular claiming endlessly to be hostile

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: irregular says the letters of the shortened word are out of order
endlessly means the last letter of claiming is dropped

explanation.surface: A guerrilla fighter asserts nonstop that he is an enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'irregular' looks like a guerrilla fighter, but it is the anagram signal working on the trimmed word.
explanation.definitionFit: Inimical means unfriendly or harmful, as an enemy would be.

clue.text: Rule enabling lecturer to accept honour in Irish capital

indicators.note: to accept means the lecturer takes in the following pieces

parts.note: a don is a university lecturer
OM is the Order of Merit, an honour

indicators.note: capital means only the first letter of Irish is taken

explanation.surface: Authority lets a lecturer take an award in Dublin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irish capital' looks like Dublin but gives only the opening letter of Irish.
explanation.definitionFit: Dominion is sovereign authority or control.

clue.text: Reportedly 14's compositions

indicators.note: Reportedly signals that the word for 14 is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: 14-down is a newspaper article also called a leader

explanation.surface: Word has it that these are works by the clue at 14.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reportedly' marks the sound-alike: LEADER, another name for 14-down's newspaper piece, sounds like the German word for songs.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieder are German art songs, such as those by Schubert.
